'''''Eriophorum angustifolium''''', commonly known as '''common cottongrass''' or '''common cottonsedge''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the sedge family, [[Cyperaceae]]. Native to [[North America]], [[North Asia]], and [[Europe]], it grows on [[peat]] or [[acidic soil]]s, in open [[wetland]], [[heath]] or [[moorland]]. It begins to flower in April or May and, after fertilisation in early summer, the small, unremarkable brown and green flowers develop distinctive white bristle-like seed-heads that resemble tufts of [[cotton]]; combined with its ecological suitability to [[bog]], these characteristics give rise to the plant's alternative name, '''bog cotton'''.

''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is a [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]], [[herbaceous]], [[rhizomatous]], [[perennial]] sedge, able to endure in a variety of environments in the temperate, subarctic and arctic regions of Earth. Unlike ''[[Gossypium]]'', the genus from which cotton is derived, the bristles of ''E. angustifolium'' are unsuited to [[textile manufacturing]]. Nevertheless, in Northern Europe, they were used as a substitute in the production of paper, pillows, candle-wicks, and wound-dressings. The [[indigenous peoples of North America]] use the plant in cooking and in the treatment of digestive problems. Following a vote in 2002, [[Plantlife|Plantlife International]] designated ''E. angustifolium'' the County Flower of [[Greater Manchester]], as part of its [[county flowers of the United Kingdom|British County Flowers campaign]].

==Description==
In the wild, ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is a creeping [[rhizomatous]] perennial sedge,{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}} with an abundance of unbranched, [[translucent]] pink roots.{{sfn|Godwin|2009|p=81}} Fully grown, it has a tall, erect stem shaped like a narrow cylinder or [[triangular prism]]; it is smooth in texture and green in colour. Reports of the plant's height vary; estimates include up to {{convert|60|cm|abbr=on}},{{sfn|Stace|2010|p=943}} {{convert|15|-|75|cm|abbr=on}},<ref>[[#Jermy|Jermy ''et al.'', 2007]]</ref> and up to {{convert|100|cm|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Ball-2002"/> ''E. angustifolium'' has "stiff grass-like foliage" consisting of long, narrow solidly dark green leaves, which have a single central groove, and narrow from their {{convert|2|-|6|mm|inch|2|adj=on}} wide base to a triangular tip.{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}}{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}} Up to seven green and brown aerial [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] and [[chaff]]s, roughly {{convert|4|-|10|mm|inch}} in size, protrude from [[umbel]]s at the top of the stem from which [[achene]]s are produced after [[fertilisation]], each with a single [[pappus (flower structure)|pappus]]; these combine to form a distinctive white [[perianth]] around {{convert|5|cm|inch}} long.{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}}<ref name="Rich-1998">{{cite web |url=http://www.bsbi.org.uk/Eriophorum_Crib_3.pdf |publisher=[[Botanical Society of the British Isles]] |title=Plant Crib: ''Eriophorum'' |access-date=16 March 2013 |year=1998 |author=Conaghan, J. P. |author2=C. Dalby |author3=M. Sheehy Skeffington |author4=T. C. G. Rich |name-list-style=amp|editor1-last=Rich |editor1-first=T. C. G. |editor2-last=Jermy |editor2-first=A. C. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021221623/http://www.bsbi.org.uk/Eriophorum_Crib_3.pdf |archive-date=21 October 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is described as "a rather dull plant" in winter and spring,{{sfn|Robinson|2003|p=97}} but "simply breathtaking" in summer and autumn,{{sfn|Lucas|2011|p=200}} when 1–7 conspicuous [[inflorescence]]s – composed of hundreds of white [[pappus (flower structure)|pappi]] comparable to [[cotton]],{{sfn|Slatcher|2012|p=83}} [[hair]],{{sfn|Godwin|2009|p=81}} [[tassel]]s,{{sfn|Robinson|2003|p=97}} and/or [[bristle]]s{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}} – stand out against naturally drab surroundings.{{sfn|Robinson|2003|p=97}}

''Eriophorum angustifolium'' differs from other species within the genus ''[[Eriophorum]]'' in its habitat and [[plant morphology|morphology]].<ref name="Rich-1998"/> Its multiple flower heads and growth from [[rhizome]]s distinguish it from ''[[Eriophorum vaginatum|E. vaginatum]]'', which has a single flower head and grows from dense [[tussock (grass)|tussocks]].<ref name="Rich-1998"/> Although ''[[Eriophorum latifolium|E. latifolium]]'' has 2–12 flower heads, it has [[Glossary of botanical terms|laxly caespitose]] (tufted) growth, and its pappi are forked.<ref name="Rich-1998"/> The smooth [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] and preference for acidic soil pH distinguishes ''E. angustifolium'' from ''[[Eriophorum gracile|E. gracile]]'', which grows in [[swamp]] with a neutral pH and has scabrid (rough) peduncles.<ref name="Rich-1998"/>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Eriophorum angustifolium Alaska USA 2022-07-20.jpg|thumb|With both terminal and axillary [[inflorescence]]s]]

The species was named ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' in 1782 by the German botanist [[Gerhard August Honckeny]].{{sfn|Mohlenbrock|2001|p=153}}{{sfn|Honckeny|1782|p=148}} The German botanist [[Albrecht Wilhelm Roth]] published this name in 1788,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/9903302 |work=Tropicos |publisher=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]] |title=''Eriophorum angustifolium'' Roth |access-date=19 March 2013}}</ref> referring to Honckeny's work,{{sfn|Roth|1788|p=24}} and is sometimes erroneously considered the author of the species name.<ref name="Phillips-1954"/> The genus name ''Eriophorum'' consists of two [[Ancient Greek]] roots – {{lang|el|εριων}} (''{{lang|el|erion}}'', "wool") and {{lang|el|[[:wikt:-φόρος|-φόρος]]}} (''{{lang|el|-phoros}}'', "-bearing"){{sfn|Runkel|Roosa|1999|p=59}} – referring to the fibrous seed-heads of the genus, which resemble tufts of thread.{{sfn|Godwin|2009|p=81}} The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''{{lang|la|angustifolium}}'' is composed of the [[Latin]] words ''{{lang|la|[[:wikt:angustus|angustus]]}}'' ("narrow") and ''{{lang|la|[[:wikt:folium|folium]]}}'' ("leaf").{{sfn|Runkel|Roosa|1999|p=59}} The [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaean]] name ''Eriophorum polystachion'' is a ''{{lang|la|[[nomen rejiciendum]]}}'',<ref name="Ball-2002">{{harvnb|Ball|Wujek|2002}}</ref> being based on a mixed batch of specimens. ''Scirpus angustifolius'' is a later combination published by the Japanese botanist [[Tetsuo Koyama]] in 1958, but this generic assignment is not widely accepted.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl/record/kew-263717 |publisher=[[The Plant List]] |title=''Scirpus angustifolius'' (Honck.) T.Koyama |access-date=19 March 2013}}</ref>

Two [[subspecies]] are recognised within ''E. angustifolium''.<ref name="Ball-2002"/> The [[autonym (botany)|autonymous]] subspecies, ''E. angustifolium'' subsp. ''angustifolium'', is found in more southerly sites, while ''E. angustifolium'' subsp. ''triste'' has an overlapping distribution centred further north.<ref name="Ball-2002"/> The two also differ in height and the roughness of the peduncles, with ''E. a.'' subsp. ''angustifolium'' being up to {{convert|100|cm|abbr=on}} tall and having smooth-surfaced peduncles, while ''E. a.'' subsp. ''triste'' has rough peduncles and only reaches {{convert|30|cm|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="Ball-2002"/>

In English, ''E. angustifolium'' is known by a variety of [[common name]]s (with various spellings), including ''common cottongrass'',{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}}{{sfn|Mabey|1996|p=389}} ''common cotton-grass'',<ref name="RHS">{{cite web |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=731 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130423222241/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=731 |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 April 2013 |author=Royal Horticultural Society |author-link=Royal Horticultural Society |title=''Eriophorum angustifolium'' |access-date=14 March 2013 |work=Plant Selector }}</ref> ''common cottonsedge'',<ref name="RHS"/> ''tassel cotton grass'',<ref name="RHS"/> ''many-headed cotton-grass'',{{sfn|Godwin|2009|p=81}} ''thin-scale cotton-grass'',{{sfn|Chadde|2012|p=88}} ''tall cotton-grass'',<ref name="NatureServe"/>{{sfn|Runkel|Roosa|1999|p=59}}{{sfn|Chadde|2012|p=128}} ''downy ling''<ref name="RHS"/> and ''bog cotton''.{{sfn|Runkel|Roosa|1999|p=59}}

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Eriophorum angustifolium distribution.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|The global distribution of ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' (green) covers large areas of northern land masses.]]

''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is native to the [[Northern Hemisphere]], and distributed across [[Eurasia]], [[North America]] and the [[British Isles]],{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}} where there is open [[bog]], [[heath]], [[wetland]] and [[moorland]], with standing water and [[calcareous]] [[peat]] or [[soil pH|acidic soil]].{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}} It can survive in the [[Subarctic]] and [[Arctic]], and is found in [[Alaska]], [[Finland]] and [[Greenland]] as far north as [[83rd parallel north|83° N]].{{sfn|Godwin|2009|p=82}}{{sfn|Evans|Warburton|2010|pp=175–176, 185–187}} The British botanist [[William Turner Thiselton-Dyer]] recorded ''E. angustifolium'' in the [[South African Republic]] in 1898.<ref name="Phillips-1954">{{harvnb|Phillips|1954}}</ref>

In North America, ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is found in the north from Alaska through [[Manitoba]] and the [[Canadian Prairies]] to [[Newfoundland and Labrador]], down the [[Pacific Northwest]] and the [[Washington (state)|state of Washington]], across the [[Midwestern United States]] through [[Michigan]] and [[Iowa]], down the [[East Coast of the United States|Eastern Seaboard]] as far south-east as [[New York (state)|New York]] and [[New Jersey]], and reaching as far south-west as [[New Mexico]].<ref name="NatureServe">{{cite web |url=http://www.natureserve.org/explorer/servlet/NatureServe?sourceTemplate=tabular_report.wmt&loadTemplate=species_RptComprehensive.wmt&selectedReport=RptComprehensive.wmt&summaryView=tabular_report.wmt&elKey=141049&paging=home&save=true&startIndex=1&nextStartIndex=1&reset=false&offPageSelectedElKey=141049&offPageSelectedElType=species&offPageYesNo=true&post_processes=&radiobutton=radiobutton&selectedIndexes=141049&selectedIndexes=159297&selectedIndexes=160753&selectedIndexes=139480 |title=''Eriophorum angustifolium'' |author=NatureServe |author-link=NatureServe |access-date=15 March 2013 }}{{Dead link|date=January 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>{{sfn|Runkel|Roosa|1999|p=59}}{{sfn|Mohlenbrock|2001|p=153}} In [[Eurasia]], ''E. angustifolium'' is distributed throughout the [[Caucasus]], [[European Russia]] and [[North Asia]], including [[Siberia]] and the [[Kamchatka Peninsula]], and south-east to [[Manchuria]] and [[Korea]].<ref name="Phillips-1954"/> It grows throughout [[continental Europe]], with the exception of those parts within the [[Mediterranean Basin]],{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}}<ref name="Phillips-1954"/> growing in [[Scandinavia]] in the north, and as far south as the [[Norte Region, Portugal|Norte Region]] of [[Portugal]] and the [[Pierian Mountains]] of [[Greece]].<ref name="Phillips-1954"/>{{sfn|Strid|Tan|1991|p=835}}

''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is the most common of the four native species of ''Eriophorum'' in the British Isles,{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}} and has been recorded as having existed in all [[Vice-county|vice-counties]],<ref name="Phillips-1954"/> thriving particularly well in [[Ireland]] and northern and western regions of Great Britain, but less so in southern and eastern areas.{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}}{{sfn|Godwin|2009|p=82}} In the [[mire]]s of [[Northern Ireland]] and the [[South Pennines]], it considered a [[Ruderal species|ruderal]], [[pioneer species|pioneer]] and [[keystone species]], because it can quickly colonise and repair damaged or eroded [[peat]], encourage the re-vegetation of its surroundings, and retain sediment and its landscape to serve as a [[carbon sink]].{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}}{{sfn|Evans|Warburton|2010|pp=175–176, 185–187}} In central and southern counties of England, the species is rare or absent,{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}} and was "completely destroyed" in [[Cambridgeshire]], [[The Broads]], [[The Fens]] and other parts of the [[East of England]] by human activities such as [[land reclamation]].{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}}{{sfn|Perring|Sell|Walters|Whitehouse|2009|pp=22, 254}} Within the British Isles, ''E. angustifolium'' thrives at a range of altitudes from sea-level [[fen]]s and lowland meadows, to exposed upland moors when provided with a habitat of acid bog or waterlogged heath.<ref name="Phillips-1954"/> It has an altitudinal limit of {{convert|1100|m|ft}} above sea level,{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}} reaching {{convert|854|m|ft}} in the [[Wicklow Mountains]] of Ireland, and {{convert|1060|m|ft|}} in the [[Scottish Highlands]].<ref name="Phillips-1954"/>

==Ecology==
[[File:Eriophorum angustifolium Tirol.jpg|thumb|right|The seeds of ''E. angustifolium'' are adapted to [[anemochory|wind-dispersal]].]]

''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is a [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]], [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]], [[rhizome|rhizomatous]], [[perennial plant]],<ref name="Phillips-1954"/> meaning that it is resilient to cold and freezing climatic conditions, dies back at the end of its [[growing season]], has creeping rootstalks, and lives for over two years. It grows vigorously from seed over a period of 2–5 years,<ref name="RHS"/> and thrives particularly well in freshly disturbed, cut or eroded [[peat]].{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}} ''E. angustifolium'' is [[Sequential hermaphroditism|protogynous]].<ref name="Phillips-1954"/>

[[Sexual reproduction]] in ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' begins with flowering in spring or early summer (in or around May), when groups of 3–5 brown flowers are produced.{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}}{{sfn|Slatcher|2012|p=83}} [[Fertilisation]] usually takes place in May or June, via [[anemophily]] (wind-pollination),<ref name="Devon Wildlife Trust">{{cite web|url=http://www.devonwildlifetrust.org/species/Cottongrass%272C+common/ |title=Species – Cottongrass, common |author=Devon Wildlife Trust |access-date=7 September 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626194134/http://www.devonwildlifetrust.org/species/Cottongrass%272C+common/ |archive-date=26 June 2015 }}</ref> and the white bristle-like perianth, composed of [[achene]]s with [[Pappus (flower structure)|pappi]] (seeds with hairs) then grows outwards to appear like short tufts of cotton thread. These pappi endure well into summer,{{sfn|Slatcher|2012|p=83}} lasting from around June to September.{{sfn|Streeter|2010|p=550}} Like the pappus of ''[[Taraxacum]]'' (dandelions), this aids in [[wind dispersal|wind-dispersal]], and also serves as [[thermal insulation]], conserving the temperature of the plant's reproductive organs by trapping solar radiation.{{sfn|Crawford|1988|pp=54–55}}

It is a known host to the [[fungus|fungal]] species ''[[Myriosclerotinia ciborium]]'', ''[[Hysteronaevia advena]]'', ''[[Lachnum imbecille]]'' and ''[[Lophodermium caricinum]]''.<ref Name="Hallgrímsson-2004">Helgi Hallgrímsson & Guðríður Gyða Eyjólfsdóttir (2004). [https://rafhladan.is/bitstream/handle/10802/4090/Fjolrit_45.pdf?sequence=1 ''Íslenskt sveppatal I – smásveppir'' [Checklist of Icelandic Fungi I – Microfungi]. Fjölrit Náttúrufræðistofnunar. Náttúrufræðistofnun Íslands [Icelandic Institute of Natural History]. ISSN 1027-832X</ref>

==Conservation==
''Eriophorum angustifolium'' has a [[NatureServe conservation status]] of G5, meaning that the species is considered to be ecologically secure by [[NatureServe]], lacking any threats to its global abundance.<ref name="NatureServe"/>

==Uses==
[[File:EangLigula.jpg|thumb|upright|right|The stem of ''Eriophorum angustifolium'', an edible part of the sedge used in [[Native American cuisine]]]]

''Eriophorum angustifolium'' seeds and stems are edible and are used in traditional [[Native American cuisine]]{{sfn|Moerman|2010|p=112}} by [[Alaska Natives]],{{sfn|Moerman|2010|p=296}} [[Inuit]] and [[Inupiat people]].{{sfn|Moerman|2010|pp=309–310}} The leaves and roots of ''E. angustifolium'' are also edible and, because of their [[astringent]] properties,{{sfn|Runkel|Roosa|1999|p=59}} used by the [[Yupik peoples]] for medicinal purposes, through a process of [[decoction]], [[infusion]] or [[poultice]], to treat ailments of the [[human gastrointestinal tract]],{{sfn|Selin|2007|p=820}} and in the [[Old World]] for the treatment of [[diarrhoea]].{{sfn|Raine|2009|p=77}} In abundance, ''E. angustifolium'' can grow with enough density to disguise wetland and [[bog]].{{sfn|Lucas|2011|p=200}} Consequently, it may be used as a natural indicator of areas which are hazardous and to avoid travelling through.{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}}{{sfn|Raine|2009|p=77}} Attempts to make a cotton-like thread from the hairs of the plant's seed-heads have been thwarted by its brittleness,{{sfn|Raine|2009|p=77}}{{sfn|Mabey|1996|p=389}} but it has been used in the production of [[paper]] and [[candle wick]]s in [[Germany]],<ref name="Devon Wildlife Trust"/>{{sfn|Graves|1822|pp=4–5}} and was used as a feather substitute in [[pillow]] stuffing in [[Sweden]]{{sfn|Graves|1822|pp=4–5}} and [[Sussex]], England.{{sfn|Mabey|1996|p=389}}{{sfn|Beardshaw|2003|p=85}} In [[Scotland]], during [[World War I]], it was used to dress wounds.{{sfn|Beardshaw|2003|p=85}}

===Cultivation===
Although "difficult to grow under cultivation",{{sfn|Runkel|Roosa|1999|p=59}} [[The Royal Horticultural Society]] states ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' can be cultivated as a low-maintenance [[wildflower]], suitable for meadows, ponds margins or [[bog garden]]s.<ref name="RHS"/> This may be done in sheltered or exposed terrain, but best accomplished with full sun at a south- or west-facing aspect, in water up to {{convert|5|cm|inch}} deep.<ref name="RHS"/> Poorly-drained [[peat]], sand, clay or [[loam]] with an acidic [[soil pH]] is required.<ref name="RHS"/> [[Division (horticulture)|Division]] in spring is the recommended form of [[plant propagation|propagation]] for the species, and regular [[Deadheading (flowers)|deadheading]] is the recommended method of [[pruning]].<ref name="RHS"/> ''[[Narthecium ossifragum]]'' and ''[[Myrica gale]]'' are suitable for [[companion planting]] with ''E. angustifolium''.{{sfn|Raven|Buckley|2012|p=352}} ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' is "generally pest free".<ref name="RHS"/> As a [[seedling]] and young plant it is eaten by [[sheep]] and [[cattle]],{{sfn|Graves|1822|pp=4–5}} and a variety of [[goose]] species.<ref>[[#Fox1990|Fox ''et al.'', 1990]]</ref> It is tolerant to [[chalybeate]] (iron-enriched) water,{{sfn|Godwin|2009|p=82}} but may succumb to [[powdery mildew]]s.<ref name="RHS"/>

==Cultural significance==
In 2002, the [[county flowers of the United Kingdom|County Flowers campaign]] of [[Plantlife|Plantlife International]], which asked members of the public to nominate and vote for a wildflower emblem for each of the counties and metropolitan areas of the United Kingdom,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3305361/Country-notebook-vote-for-the-poppy.html|work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|title=Country notebook: vote for the poppy|first=Germaine|last=Greer|author-link=Germaine Greer|date=5 October 2002|access-date=15 March 2013}}</ref> resulted in ''Eriophorum angustifolium'' being announced as the County Flower of [[Greater Manchester]].<ref name="Lashley-2003">{{cite web |title=So what bloom best suits you? |url=http://menmedia.co.uk/manchestereveningnews/news/s/54/54214_so_what_bloom_best_suits_you.html |last=Lashley |first=Brian |access-date=7 September 2012 |date=20 March 2003 |work=[[Manchester Evening News]] |archive-date=21 April 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130421044152/http://menmedia.co.uk/manchestereveningnews/news/s/54/54214_so_what_bloom_best_suits_you.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Plantlife">{{cite web |url=http://www.plantlife.org.uk/things_to_do/regions/north_west |title=North-west England |author=Plantlife International |author-link=Plantlife |access-date=7 September 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130501110914/http://www.plantlife.org.uk/things_to_do/regions/north_west/ |archive-date=1 May 2013 }}</ref>
